title: What problems did you encounter when scaling? What tools helped you solve it?
author: New_Patience_8107
selftext:
I'm building a game in Godot think GTA lite but with a deep strategy and simulation element behind it. That means I need an open world where it's as fun shooting as it is spending 20 mins planning your next steps out at a home base.

At first I was killing it development wise. I had a roadmap plan and thought I had covered corners but it's a monster that gets bigger and bigger. Before you know it I've solved a problem but then see five gapping holes that need filling before moving on.

I'm realizing I need to stop and building tooling that will teach my AI to fish. Take assets for example. Getting one building from image to meshly to then have Claude put the finishing touch is taking hours and most of my 5 hour window. I need to come up with clever ways to generate many buildings without every build being from zero. So I'll look at building some procedural generator assuming there's nothing out there I can build off.

What scaling problems did you face and what tool did you need to bring in to fix it?

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body: I never ran into production pipeline bottleneck problems because Astra is so good at building little micro-tools it is actually crazy.

comments.author: YuukiCrypto
comments.body: It is called scope creep. In your case, its not so much scope creep because you said you wanted to make a GTA lite. That means you have a huge scope. You know how long we have been waiting for GTA 6...

replies.author: New_Patience_8107
replies.body: Emphasis on the lite. It's really just some third person shooting with squads and some strategy style elements on top. Still it's a project and scope changes in a project.

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body:
Want something helpful?Q

Write down 1-4 rules this will be your lenses on all the game features, these rules would describe what game you want to make. These would by your game design pillars.

Any time you add a feature it should satisfy these rules. More is not always better, if your feature has many holes maybe it is too complex or it has many dependencies. (This may mean it will be hard to comprehend for players too.)

I would suggest to build a vertical slice with minimum graphics and solid gameplay following your game design pillars. I would suggest to keep the features on minimum and add new features only if they are mandatory for your core loop. (Later you can add the fluff feature when the game loop is fun.) Do not add a features because Claude or Codex suggest it, look at the feature from the pillars perspective and how much player value they bring. Every new feature will make your code more complex and harder to handle(and will make AI iterations more expensive). 

There is no magical solution for this, if you do not want to make slop it will take time and AI is not great in design decisions, so you need to make them and there are many of them. 

Keep it simple and just focus on core, if the core is fun branch of from it and you have the first playable version of the game, even if you later add tons of features and make it mess, you can come back to this simple and fun version.

replies.author: New_Patience_8107
replies.body: This was actually helpful thank you.

comments.author: StatisticianSoft9052
comments.body: i tried to build open world game in godot, got somewhat far but constantly run into cpu issues. Did a lot of cpu optimizing iterations and finally realized godots advantage is fast build time, but it is not the right choice for huge maps with a lot of objects. Then i switched to unreal, porting all CPU optimizitaion and everything. Complete rewrite, but well. Unreals world Partitioning is the solution for all CPU pain. Unreal does asset triangle downscaling out of the box, flawless, better then Blender. like Lense flare effect? Just check a box.

replies.author: New_Patience_8107
replies.body:
Interesting feedback cheets. My solution for the large map and objects is a sort of view only within a certain radius of the chosen character and everything else should just be background data or a sprite. I try to stress test full scenes with 50 NPCs shooting at each other and have identified things already which would've blown everything up.

Still though won't know what it's running like until I get that far. Could imagine rebuilding the whole thing afterwards in C# somewhere at the end.

replies.author: StatisticianSoft9052
replies.body:
your game has to pre-load/calculate this data in background cpu threads when your character is moving to different areas. this adds up to more cpu load, i have 16x 3,8Ghz it just drove me nuts at some point, i couldnt have the amount of coconut trees i wanted in godot. unreal is c++ and its main disatvange is building time ( and code complexity which is irrelevant for ai agent ). tradeoff for high end looks and top performance, for your openworld gta game its obvious choice i think.

unfortunately my rtx 3060 isnt strong enough for raytracing, but even without raytracing its a noticable difference. have 2 youtube videos of both working editions if you want to take a look: Godot [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Um7quWbNGeQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Um7quWbNGeQ)  Unreal  [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i2K0X8va3aU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i2K0X8va3aU)

replies.author: egonosz
replies.body: Tbh. You can use c++ with godot and I would not say code complexity is irrelevant, because after a time it will slow down the agents.
